questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Cardiac output is the product of:
questions.concept: Normal output is about 5 L/min. Cardiac index adjusts for body surface area, and the determinants of stroke volume are preload, afterload and contractility.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Cardiac output is measured by the Fick principle using:
options: Oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference
questions.concept: Thermodilution using a pulmonary artery catheter and echocardiographic methods are the practical clinical alternatives, with echocardiography now predominant because it is non-invasive.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs mainly during:
questions.concept: Systolic myocardial compression obstructs left coronary flow, so tachycardia shortening diastole and aortic stenosis reducing perfusion pressure both precipitate ischaemia even with normal coronaries.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Cerebral blood flow is autoregulated over a mean arterial pressure range of approximately:
questions.concept: The range shifts rightward in chronic hypertension, so rapid lowering of blood pressure can cause cerebral hypoperfusion - which is why blood pressure is reduced gradually in hypertensive emergency.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The most potent physiological stimulus increasing cerebral blood flow is:
options: A rise in arterial carbon dioxide tension
questions.concept: Hypercapnia causes cerebral vasodilatation, which is why hyperventilation is used briefly to lower intracranial pressure. Prolonged hyperventilation risks ischaemia from excessive vasoconstriction.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: During exercise, the increase in cardiac output is achieved mainly by:
options: Increased heart rate, with stroke volume plateauing at moderate intensity
questions.concept: Total peripheral resistance falls as skeletal muscle vessels dilate, so mean pressure rises only modestly while systolic pressure and pulse pressure increase substantially.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The skin circulation is unique in serving primarily:
options: Thermoregulation, via arteriovenous anastomoses under sympathetic control
questions.concept: Cutaneous flow can vary from near zero to 30% of cardiac output. Loss of this vasoconstrictor response contributes to the warm peripheries and hypotension of septic shock.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The ejection fraction is calculated as:
options: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally 55 to 70 percent
Stroke volume divided by cardiac output
questions.concept: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction below 40% is distinguished from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, which reflects diastolic dysfunction and requires different management.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The baroreceptor reflex responds to a fall in blood pressure by:
options: Reducing vagal tone and increasing sympathetic outflow, raising rate and resistance
questions.concept: Carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch receptors signal via glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. This buffer reflex resets in chronic hypertension, which is why it does not correct sustained hypertension.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Central venous pressure principally reflects:
options: Right atrial pressure and therefore right ventricular preload and volume status
questions.concept: It is raised in right heart failure, tamponade, tension pneumothorax and fluid overload, and low in hypovolaemia. Trends in response to fluid challenge are more informative than single readings.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Gastric acid is secreted by:
options: Parietal (oxyntic) cells, which also secrete intrinsic factor
questions.concept: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, G cells gastrin and D cells somatostatin. Loss of parietal cells in autoimmune atrophic gastritis causes both achlorhydria and pernicious anaemia from intrinsic factor deficiency.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The three stimulants of gastric acid secretion acting on the parietal cell are:
questions.concept: Histamine acting on H2 receptors is the final common amplifier, which is why H2 blockers are effective; proton pump inhibitors act further downstream on the H+/K+ ATPase and are more powerful.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Secretin is released from the duodenum in response to:
questions.concept: Cholecystokinin is released by fat and protein, causing gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation and pancreatic enzyme secretion - a useful pairing to remember with secretin.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Vitamin B12 absorption requires intrinsic factor and occurs in:
questions.concept: This is why terminal ileal resection or Crohn disease causes B12 deficiency, whereas iron and folate are absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum, explaining the pattern of deficiency after different resections.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Bile salts are essential for absorption of:
options: Fat and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
questions.concept: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled through the enterohepatic circulation. Ileal disease therefore causes both steatorrhoea and bile-salt diarrhoea.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The migrating motor complex functions to:
options: Sweep undigested residue and bacteria along the gut during fasting
questions.concept: Governed by motilin and abolished by feeding, it is the intestinal housekeeper. Its impairment contributes to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth in diabetic autonomic neuropathy and scleroderma.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The primary site of water absorption in the gastrointestinal tract is:
options: The small intestine, with the colon absorbing the remainder
questions.concept: About 8 to 9 litres enter the small bowel daily of which most is absorbed there, leaving 1 to 2 litres for the colon which absorbs all but about 100 mL - hence small bowel disease causes voluminous diarrhoea.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Glucose absorption from the intestinal lumen occurs by:
options: Sodium-coupled secondary active transport via SGLT1
questions.concept: This is the physiological basis of oral rehydration solution, in which glucose drives sodium and hence water absorption even when secretory diarrhoea is active.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The enterohepatic circulation is clinically important because:
options: Interruption by ileal disease or resin binding increases cholesterol excretion and causes fat malabsorption
questions.concept: Bile acid sequestrants exploit it to lower cholesterol by forcing hepatic conversion of cholesterol to new bile acids. It also prolongs the action of drugs undergoing biliary recycling.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Saliva has which principal digestive function?
options: Starch digestion by salivary amylase, with lubrication and antibacterial action
questions.concept: Saliva is hypotonic with high potassium and bicarbonate. It also contains lysozyme, lactoferrin and IgA, which is why xerostomia predisposes to dental caries and oral candidiasis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Gastrointestinal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The most abundant hormone secreted by the thyroid gland is:
options: Thyroxine (T4), which is converted peripherally to the more active T3
questions.concept: About 80% of circulating T3 comes from peripheral deiodination of T4. Propylthiouracil, propranolol, corticosteroids and severe illness inhibit this conversion, raising inactive reverse T3.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis, and its trapping is inhibited by:
questions.concept: Carbimazole and propylthiouracil instead inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking organification and coupling. High-dose iodide acutely inhibits release - the Wolff-Chaikoff effect used before thyroid surgery.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Cortisol secretion shows a diurnal rhythm with a peak:
options: In the early morning around 6 to 8 am
questions.concept: The midnight nadir is why a raised late-night salivary cortisol is a sensitive screen for Cushing syndrome, and why replacement is given as a larger morning dose.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Aldosterone secretion is primarily regulated by:
questions.concept: ACTH has only a permissive role, which is why aldosterone secretion is largely preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease, unlike primary Addison disease where it is lost.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Insulin secretion from the beta cell is triggered by:
options: Glucose metabolism raising ATP, closing K-ATP channels and causing calcium influx
questions.concept: Sulfonylureas close the same K-ATP channel independently of glucose, which is why they cause hypoglycaemia whereas metformin, which does not stimulate secretion, does not.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The principal action of parathyroid hormone on the kidney is:
options: Increased calcium reabsorption and increased phosphate excretion
questions.concept: PTH also stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase producing active vitamin D. The combination of high calcium with low phosphate and raised PTH characterises primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Active vitamin D (calcitriol) is formed by hydroxylation in the:
options: Liver at position 25 and kidney at position 1
questions.concept: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation is the regulated step stimulated by PTH and hypophosphataemia. Its loss in chronic kidney disease causes hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Calcitonin from thyroid C cells:
options: Lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, but has minor physiological importance in humans
questions.concept: Neither thyroidectomy nor medullary carcinoma with very high calcitonin disturbs calcium significantly, showing its limited physiological role, though it is a valuable tumour marker.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Growth hormone exerts most of its growth-promoting effects through:
options: Insulin-like growth factor 1 produced by the liver
questions.concept: IGF-1 mediates linear growth and is a stable index of GH status, unlike pulsatile GH itself. Laron dwarfism results from GH receptor resistance with high GH but low IGF-1.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: The counter-regulatory hormones opposing insulin include:
options: Glucagon, cortisol, growth hormone and adrenaline
questions.concept: Glucagon and adrenaline act within minutes while cortisol and growth hormone act over hours. Their unopposed action in insulin deficiency drives the lipolysis and ketogenesis of diabetic ketoacidosis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Endocrinology
